explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The verse says it plainly: "He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted." That comes right after the promise that the Servant will prosper (Isaiah 52:13). Starting with good news is a smart move, because the next verse gets hard.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: I get the doubt, friend, because the very next verse gets hard. But verse 13 says it straight: "He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted." The Servant will prosper and also be lifted up. Hold onto that one while the passage moves along.

explanations.answer: Disfigured beyond that of any man
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says "…His appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man, and His form was marred beyond human likeness…" Many were appalled at Him (Isaiah 52:14). It's a hard picture, and I think it's meant to be.

explanations.answer: Bright like the face of an angel
explanations.explanation: I can see why a bright face sounds nice, friend, but that's not what the verse says. It says many were appalled at Him because His appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man. Nothing here shines like an angel. The Servant is shown as marred.

explanations.answer: Dressed like a king on his throne
explanations.explanation: A throne would be a nice touch, friend, but the verse doesn't have one. It says many were appalled at Him because His appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man (Isaiah 52:14). Later the people speaking say He had "…no stately form or majesty to attract us…" (Isaiah 53:2). That's the picture the text gives.

explanations.answer: They will see what they were never told
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The text says "…they will see what they have not been told, and they will understand what they have not heard." The kings go quiet because of what they see and understand (Isaiah 52:15). Picture a room full of important people suddenly out of words.

explanations.answer: They will lose a war against Israel
explanations.explanation: No war shows up in these verses, friend. The reason is about seeing. "For they will see what they have not been told, and they will understand what they have not heard." That's why the kings shut their mouths (Isaiah 52:15).

explanations.answer: He will order them to keep quiet
explanations.explanation: The text never has the Servant giving an order, friend. The kings shut their mouths "…because of Him." and the reason given is what they see and understand. "…they will see what they have not been told…" (Isaiah 52:15). Their silence comes from what they've seen.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. When someone asks "Who has believed our message?" I think it sounds like not many have (Isaiah 53:1). A question like that doesn't sound like a crowd cheering. The second question, about to whom the arm of the LORD has been revealed, keeps going in that direction.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. "Who has believed our message?" doesn't sound like everyone already believes it. I think it sounds more like somebody looking around and wondering who's on board. It's followed by another question: "And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?" (Isaiah 53:1).

explanations.answer: Nothing in His looks drew people in
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The text says "He had no stately form or majesty to attract us, no beauty that we should desire Him." He grew up like a tender shoot, like a root out of dry ground (Isaiah 53:2). It's a plain, humble picture.

explanations.answer: He looked like a king in a palace
explanations.explanation: A palace would be fancy, friend, but the verse says the opposite. "He had no stately form or majesty to attract us…" The picture is a tender shoot and a root out of dry ground (Isaiah 53:2). No crown and no marble floors here.

explanations.answer: Crowds came just to see His face
explanations.explanation: Crowds coming to see His face isn't in the verse, friend. It says He had "…no stately form or majesty to attract us, no beauty that we should desire Him." (Isaiah 53:2). Nothing in His looks pulled people in.

explanations.answer: faces
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The verse says "Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised, and we esteemed Him not." He was treated like someone men hide their faces from (Isaiah 53:3). I think that's the heavy part.

explanations.answer: children
explanations.explanation: Children don't show up in this verse, friend. The text says "Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised…" He was treated like someone men hide their faces from (Isaiah 53:3). It's about faces.

explanations.answer: money
explanations.explanation: People hide money all the time, friend. I once hid a whole tray of cookies behind the mixer. But the verse is about something else: "Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised…" (Isaiah 53:3). It's faces, not money.

explanations.answer: That God had struck Him down
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The people speaking say, "…we considered Him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted." But the same verse says He "…took up our infirmities and carried our sorrows…" (Isaiah 53:4). They saw one thing, and the verse tells us something deeper.

explanations.answer: That He was hiding from God
explanations.explanation: Hiding isn't in this verse, friend. The people speaking say, "…we considered Him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted." That's what they thought was happening to Him (Isaiah 53:4). The verse never says He ran from God.

explanations.answer: That He was faking His pain
explanations.explanation: Nobody says anything about faking, friend. The people speaking say, "…we considered Him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted." His pain is treated as real. What they thought was that God had struck Him down (Isaiah 53:4).

explanations.answer: Servant
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says "the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him…" The Servant was pierced and crushed, and the peace comes to the people speaking (Isaiah 53:5). That's the turn in the whole passage.

explanations.answer: nations
explanations.explanation: The nations show up earlier, friend, but not here. In Isaiah 52:15 the Servant will sprinkle many nations. In 53:5 the text says "the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him…" The punishment fell on the Servant.

explanations.answer: kings
explanations.explanation: Kings do show up in Isaiah 52:15, friend, where they shut their mouths because of Him. But in 53:5 the text says "the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him…" The Servant is the one who "…was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities…" (Isaiah 53:5). The punishment landed on Him.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The verse says "…by His stripes we are healed." The people speaking say it about themselves (Isaiah 53:5). It lands right after the pierced and crushed part, and it's a hopeful line.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: It really does say that, friend. The verse says "…by His stripes we are healed." Stripes are the marks left on someone who has been beaten. The people speaking say it about themselves, right after saying He was pierced and crushed (Isaiah 53:5). His stripes come first, and the healing is theirs.

explanations.answer: He lays it all on the Servant
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The text says "…the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all." Everyone had gone astray, and the weight went onto the Servant (Isaiah 53:6). Notice the word all.

explanations.answer: He leaves each one to carry it
explanations.explanation: You'd expect that, friend, since each one turned to his own way. But the verse says something different. "…the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all." The wrong goes onto the Servant (Isaiah 53:6).

explanations.answer: He sends it away with the sheep
explanations.explanation: The sheep are only in the picture of how people wandered, friend. The verse says, "We all like sheep have gone astray…" Then it says where the wrong goes: "…the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all." (Isaiah 53:6). It's laid on the Servant.

explanations.answer: A lamb led to the slaughter
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The text says, "He was led like a lamb to the slaughter…" It adds that "…as a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth." (Isaiah 53:7). He stays quiet through all of it.

explanations.answer: A goat sent into the wilderness
explanations.explanation: A goat isn't what this verse uses, friend. The animal here is a lamb. "He was led like a lamb to the slaughter…" And a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth (Isaiah 53:7).

explanations.answer: A ram caught in a thicket
explanations.explanation: A ram in a thicket is a fine picture, friend, but it's from another story (Genesis 22:13). In Isaiah 53:7 the pictures are a lamb and a sheep. "He was led like a lamb to the slaughter…" That's the animal for this verse.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The verse says "He was stricken for the transgression of My people." It's their transgression, not His own (Isaiah 53:8). And verse 9 adds that He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The text says "He was stricken for the transgression of My people." It was their transgression that He was stricken for (Isaiah 53:8). And verse 9 says there was no deceit in His mouth.

explanations.answer: He did no violence and told no lies
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says "…although He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth." He was assigned a grave with the wicked even so (Isaiah 53:9). I think that makes the line hit harder.

explanations.answer: He fought back against His enemies
explanations.explanation: No fighting here, friend. The verse says "…He had done no violence…" (Isaiah 53:9). And another verse says He did not open His mouth (Isaiah 53:7). Nothing in the passage shows Him fighting back.

explanations.answer: He hid the truth to stay safe
explanations.explanation: That one flips the verse, friend. The text says "…nor was any deceit in His mouth." Whatever He said, there was no deceit in it (Isaiah 53:9). Hiding the truth isn't part of this picture.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The verse says "…when His soul is made a guilt offering, He will see His offspring, He will prolong His days…" It comes right after the heavy line about the LORD's will to crush Him (Isaiah 53:10). The verse doesn't stop at the hard part.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: It's easy to think so after such a heavy line, friend. But the verse says "…when His soul is made a guilt offering, He will see His offspring, He will prolong His days…" That's what happens after the hard part (Isaiah 53:10). Good news is still coming.

explanations.answer: Justify them and bear their iniquities
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says "By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities." It's the same carrying we saw earlier in the passage (Isaiah 53:11). He does it for many.

explanations.answer: Judge them and send them away
explanations.explanation: Sending away isn't what the verse says, friend. It says "…My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities." He bears their iniquities (Isaiah 53:11). That's the opposite of sending them off.

explanations.answer: Teach them and then leave them
explanations.explanation: Leaving isn't in this verse, friend. The text says "By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities." Bearing iniquities is staying with the weight, not walking away (Isaiah 53:11). That's the Servant's work for many.

explanations.answer: He poured out His life unto death
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The text says "…because He has poured out His life unto death…" That's the reason He gets a portion with the great (Isaiah 53:12). The reason isn't a win. It's that He poured out His life.

explanations.answer: He won a battle against the strong
explanations.explanation: Winning a battle sounds like a good reason, friend, but the verse gives another one. It says "…because He has poured out His life unto death…" He divides the spoils with the strong, but no battle is mentioned (Isaiah 53:12).

explanations.answer: He ruled over many nations
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess, friend, but the verse gives a different reason. It says "…because He has poured out His life unto death…" Nothing here says He ruled over nations (Isaiah 53:12). The reason is the pouring out.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The last words of the passage say "Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors." He was numbered with them, and He also made intercession for them (Isaiah 53:12). That's a good place to end.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Look at the very last line, friend. It says "Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors." Intercession means speaking up on someone's behalf. So He was numbered with the transgressors, and He also spoke up for them (Isaiah 53:12).
